summary: Indonesian-language paper setting out a philosophical framework for practice-based research in art and visual design, contrasting its paradigm — the practitioner as researcher, knowledge as inter-subjective and context-bound — with natural- and social-science research. Open access, published in Humaniora (Bina Nusantara University).
relevance: A Southeast Asian artistic-research methodology text, filling the atlas's stated coverage gap in artistic-research primary texts from Asia.

author: Ramunė Balevičiūtė
work: Promises of artistic research and its actuality. Artistic research in theatre
summary: Questions whether the promise of artistic research as a new academic paradigm matches its actual practice, examining the concept's persistent lack of shared definition and the particular tensions it raises in theatre and performance research. Menotyra 24(2), 2017; open access, English-language PDF.
relevance: A critical counter-voice from inside the field to the atlas's founding methodology texts (Frayling, Borgdorff) — it interrogates the artistic-research paradigm rather than advocating for it.

author: Hadiyan Yusuf Kuntoro
work: Glitch Art Sebagai Refleksi Memori Manusia yang Rapuh: Sebuah Penciptaan Karya Seni
summary: Documents the making of a glitch-art work through nine creative-process stages, 'data-bending' digital image data with an audio editor (Audacity) as a metaphor for fragile human memory. Gorga: Jurnal Seni Rupa 13(1), 2024 (Indonesian; open access, CC BY-SA).
relevance: A first-person practice-based account of technical error deliberately induced and turned into method — extends the atlas's coverage of artistic-research primary texts from Southeast Asia, a stated gap.

author: Arianna Gass
work: Glitch as a Trans Representational Mode in Video Games
summary: Reads three video games' use of glitch aesthetics — remediated signal noise and error — as a representational mode for transgender embodiment, dissociation and dysphoria, distinct from broader queer-games frameworks. Media-N 20(1), 2024; open access, CC BY-SA.
relevance: Treats glitch not as failure but as a generative expressive method, the same register the atlas already holds for Menkman's glitch studies, here applied to trans representation in games.

author: Giorgio Franceschelli, Mirco Musolesi
work: On the Creativity of Large Language Models
summary: Applies Boden's novelty/value/surprise framework and the classic four-P model (product, process, press, person) to large language models to ask whether they can be considered creative, separating 'easy' from 'hard' problems in machine creativity. Published in AI & Society, open access (CC-BY).
relevance: Gives the atlas a philosophically grounded account of what would have to be true for a machine to count as creative, the theoretical counterpart to the self-consuming-loop findings already anchored here.

author: Anna Jordanous, Bill Keller
work: Modelling Creativity: Identifying Key Components through a Corpus-Based Approach
summary: Uses statistical NLP on a corpus of creativity-research writing to derive fourteen components that recur across definitions of creativity, building a corpus-grounded model for evaluating computational-creativity systems. Published in PLOS ONE, open access (CC-BY).
relevance: A method for deriving creativity from evidence rather than stipulation, ballast against asserting creativity in the atelier's own works rather than measuring it.

author: Ahmad Beltagui, Andrew Bell, Marina Candi
work: A Sociomaterial Perspective on Epistemic Objects in Design Practice
summary: Field interviews across three design organizations identify four characteristics, fidelity, investment, ambiguity, history, that make an artefact function as an epistemic object holding a team's incomplete knowledge open rather than closing it. Published in Design Studies, open access (CC-BY).
relevance: Extends Rheinberger's epistemic-things line, already anchored here, from the laboratory into design practice, a direct bridge for a session that treats its own working notebook as an epistemic object.

author: Laila Rosa, Isabel Nogueira
work: O que nos move, o que nos dobra, o que nos instiga: notas sobre epistemologias feministas, processos criativos, educação e possibilidades transgressoras em música
summary: Two composer-performers examine their own songwriting through postcolonial feminist epistemologies, using their creative process to discuss gender and racial exclusion in music and academia. Portuguese-language article in Revista Vórtex, open access (CC BY 4.0), with accompanying audio files.
relevance: Fills the atlas's flagged gap in Latin American artistic-research voices and ties feminist epistemology directly to a documented creative process rather than to theory alone.

author: Craig Batty, Marsha Berry
work: Constellations and Connections: The Playful Space of the Creative Practice Research Degree
summary: Examines how doctoral candidates in creative-practice research move between conceptual thinking and material production, arguing the resulting space is productively messy rather than a failure of rigor. Published in Journal of Media Practice, open access (CC-BY) via Figshare.
relevance: A methodology text on tolerating unresolved, playful process, the institutional counterpart to the atelier's own refusal to treat an unfinished session as failure.

author: Duncan Pritchard
work: Ignorance and Inquiry
summary: Argues against standard accounts that define ignorance as mere absence of knowledge or true belief, proposing instead that ignorance is an intellectual failing of inquiry itself. Published in American Philosophical Quarterly; the journal version is paywalled, but the given repository URL hosts a free accepted-manuscript PDF.
relevance: Sharpens the atlas's not-knowing axis with a contemporary analytic account of what ignorance is, alongside Firestein's practitioner view and Cusanus's docta ignorantia.

author: M. Beatrice Fazi
work: Can a machine think (anything new)? Automation beyond simulation
summary: Reworks the classical question 'Can a machine think?' into 'Can a machine think anything new?', arguing via Leibniz's mathesis universalis and Turing's computation that machine thought must be assessed on its own onto-epistemological terms rather than as simulation of human cognition. Published in AI & SOCIETY; open access.
relevance: Gives the atlas's machine-creativity question philosophical teeth beyond behavioural tests: not whether a machine seems creative, but whether automated thought can be genuinely novel at all.

author: Mark Coeckelbergh
work: Can Machines Create Art?
summary: Breaks 'Can machines create art?' into sub-questions about art creation, art, and machine authorship, showing that process/outcome and subjective/objective criteria of creativity are unstable, and extends the question to human-machine collaboration. Published in Philosophy & Technology; open access.
relevance: A conceptual companion to Boden and Hertzmann already in the atlas, pushing the machine-creativity debate from criteria-hunting toward the human/non-human encounter itself.

author: Mira Kallio-Tavin, Heidi Fast, Kirsi Heimonen, Tiina Pusa & Riitta Hari
work: Touched And Moved By Arts: Introduction to a Transdisciplinary Discourse on Human Experience
summary: Introduction to a transdisciplinary special issue arguing that artistic research addresses experiences difficult to grasp conceptually, drawing on neuroscientific concepts (predictive processing, interoception) alongside embodied case studies (nonverbal vocal art, painting, extremely slow-speed walking) to verbalise rich artistic experience. Published in Research in Arts and Education; open access.
relevance: Names the atelier's own problem directly, how to put into words a knowledge that resists concepts, and does it through practice-based cases rather than abstract theory.

author: Desmond Bell
work: The Primacy of Practice: Establishing the Terms of Reference of Creative Arts and Media Research
summary: Defines the key terms of practice-based arts and media research and situates the endeavour within its institutional setting, reviewing the forms of arts research currently practised in higher education. Book chapter; open access.
relevance: A terminology-setting text for practice-as-research that sharpens what the atelier can claim when it calls its own practice research.

author: Catharina Dyrssen
work: Artistic research: A subject overview 2014
summary: Official Swedish national overview describing artistic research as an academic subject area, held at Chalmers University of Technology's publication library. Paywalled: the given URL is a verified metadata record documenting existence and location, not a direct full-text link.
relevance: A canonical Nordic institutional definition of the field the atelier operates within, alongside Frayling and Borgdorff already anchored in the atlas.

author: Xiaodan Xing, Fadong Shi, Jiahao Huang, Yinzhe Wu, Yang Nan, Sheng Zhang, Yingying Fang, Mike Roberts, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, Javier Del Ser & Guang Yang
work: On the caveats of AI autophagy
summary: Perspective piece naming and surveying 'AI autophagy' — the unregulated spread of AI-generated content online, which increasingly contaminates the web-scraped datasets used to train newer generative models, risking degraded performance and reliability. Published in Nature Machine Intelligence; paywalled at the publisher, but the given URL is an open-access, CC-BY accepted-manuscript copy in Imperial College's repository.
relevance: Broadens the atlas's self-consuming-loop literature (Shumailov, Gerstgrasser, Jangjoo/Marsili/Roudi) from a single controlled-experiment result to a survey of the phenomenon across modalities and its mitigation strategies.

author: Javier Conde, M. Ángeles González, Gonzalo Martínez, Fernando Moral, Elena Merino-Gómez & Pedro Reviriego
work: Recursive InPainting (RIP): how much information is lost under recursive inferences?
summary: Empirical study applying Stable Diffusion's inpainting recursively to the same image — removing a fragment, reconstructing it, removing another, repeating — and measuring how much visual information is lost or drifts across iterations. Published in AI & SOCIETY; open access.
relevance: An image-based sibling to Shumailov's text-based 'curse of recursion' — the same self-consuming-loop degradation demonstrated one modality over, useful for the atelier's cross-media argument about closed loops.

author: Paul Draper & Scott Harrison
work: Through the eye of a needle: the emergence of a practice-led research doctorate in music
summary: Case study of a practice-led doctoral programme at an Australian conservatoire, examining its blended research-training structure (supervision, coursework, web-based tools) and the challenges and opportunities as such programmes expand. Published in the British Journal of Music Education; open access.
relevance: An institutional counterpart to the atlas's more philosophical practice-as-research texts — shows how a practice-led doctorate was actually built and run, not only argued for.

author: Martin Blain & Helen Julia Minors (eds.)
work: Artistic Research in Performance through Collaboration
summary: Edited volume (Palgrave Macmillan / Springer) collecting essays on collaborative artistic-research practice in musical and theatrical performance. Paywalled at the publisher; no freely retrievable full text located.
relevance: Extends the atlas's practice-as-research line into collaborative performance practice specifically, alongside Coessens/Crispin/Douglas and de Assis already anchored here.

author: Katja Brøgger & Miriam Madsen
work: An Affirmative-Diffractive Re-Reading of the Policy Instrumentation Approach through Agential Realism and the Accreditation Instrument
summary: Rereads the Lascoumes/Le Galès policy-instrumentation approach through Barad's agential realism, applying diffraction as method to the case of higher-education accreditation. Journal of Education Policy, 2021. Gold open access (accepted manuscript held at Aarhus University's repository), though both the publisher page and the repository PDF sit behind a bot challenge that blocks automated fetching.
relevance: A second worked example of Barad's diffraction as method, alongside Hickey-Moody et al. already in the atlas — here applied to institutional policy rather than pedagogy, widening the diffraction tag's range.

author: Timote Masima Vaioleti
work: Talanoa Research Methodology: A Developing Position on Pacific Research
summary: Develops talanoa — a Tongan/Pacific conversational method — into a research methodology in its own right, set against imported Western frameworks. Waikato Journal of Education, Vol. 12 (2006); the journal's online reissue on its current platform is dated 2016, which is what most indexers show. Open access, direct PDF.
relevance: A non-Western research methodology standing next to Tuhiwai Smith and Santos already in the atlas — narrows the atlas's own noted coverage gap in methodology texts from outside the European canon.

author: Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni
work: Global Coloniality and the Challenges of Creating African Futures
summary: Argues that global coloniality persists as an invisible power matrix constraining African epistemic and political agency, asking what an autonomous African future would require against it. The Strategic Review for Southern Africa, Vol. 36 No. 2 (2014); the journal's online reissue on its current platform is dated 2020, which is what most indexers show. Open access (CC BY-NC-SA).
relevance: Extends the atlas's decolonial cluster (Santos, Mignolo/Vázquez, Tuhiwai Smith) with an Africa-centred argument, addressing the same coverage gap the atlas README names.

author: Julian McDougall
work: But How Is It Not Just Practice? Or Do I Not Know Practice as Research?
summary: Essay in Alphaville: Journal of Film and Screen Media (no. 17, pp. 26–37) arguing that practice-based media research must show originality, significance and rigour as new knowledge rather than being read as vocational craft — and that making this case is itself a political project against academic hierarchies that marginalise creative practitioners. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND).
relevance: Poses practice-as-research's legitimacy question as a question of not-knowing in its own title — a direct bridge between the atelier's swerve method-philosophy and the practice-as-research debate the atlas already anchors (Frayling, Borgdorff, Nelson).

author: Mark A. Runco
work: AI Can Only Produce Artificial Creativity
summary: Article in Journal of Creativity (vol. 33, no. 3, 100063) arguing that generative AI systems recombine and remix existing patterns rather than originate genuinely novel ideas, so calling their output 'creative' collapses a distinction worth keeping. Open access (gold, CC BY-NC-ND, DOAJ-listed).
relevance: A skeptical counterweight inside the atlas's machine-creativity cluster (Boden, Coeckelbergh, Fazi already anchored) — the position Error as Method has to argue against when it claims machinic drift produces more than recombination.

author: Tony Veale & Rafael Pérez y Pérez
work: Leaps and Bounds: An Introduction to the Field of Computational Creativity
summary: Introduction in New Generation Computing (vol. 38, no. 4, pp. 551–563) surveying computational creativity as a research field — its founding questions and its disagreements over what counts as a creative system. Open access (publisher-hosted free PDF; bronze, no explicit reuse licence).
relevance: A field-level orientation text for the atlas's computational-creativity cluster, giving the disciplinary frame the other machine-creativity entries argue inside of.

author: Caterina Moruzzi
work: Measuring Creativity: An Account of Natural and Artificial Creativity
summary: Article in European Journal for Philosophy of Science (vol. 11, no. 1) proposing an account of creativity — novelty, value and intentionality together — that applies consistently to human and artificial systems alike, then uses it to assess where current AI systems fall short. Open access (gold, CC BY).
relevance: Supplies the atlas's machine-creativity cluster with a working definition against which Runco's skepticism and the atelier's own claims about machinic creativity can both be tested.

author: Filippo Carnovalini & Antonio Rodà
work: Computational Creativity and Music Generation Systems: An Introduction to the State of the Art
summary: Review in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence (vol. 3) surveying algorithmic approaches to music generation — Markov chains, formal grammars, neural networks, genetic algorithms — against theories of creativity, and naming persistent open problems such as structural coherence and evaluation. Open access (gold, CC BY).
relevance: Names the stochastic and evolutionary methods actually used to generate machine creativity — concrete technical ground under the atelier's own claims about chance-driven, aleatoric generation.

author: Francisco Varela, Humberto R. Maturana & R. Uribe
work: Autopoiesis: The Organization of Living Systems, Its Characterization and a Model
summary: The original paper in BioSystems (vol. 5, no. 4) that formally introduces autopoiesis — Varela, Maturana and Uribe give the concept its first rigorous definition and a cellular-automaton model of self-producing organization. Open access (full-text PDF via the Universidad de Chile repository).
relevance: Completes the atlas's cybernetics anchor at its source: the atelier already carries Maturana/Varela's 1980 book, but the concept was coined here first, six years earlier, in the primary journal record.

author: Dejan Grba
work: Art Notions in the Age of (Mis)anthropic AI
summary: Article in Arts (vol. 13, no. 5) arguing that generative AI carries tech-industry ideologies — machinic-agency fetishism, human/machine equalization, cyberlibertarianism — into contemporary art discourse under the cover of a democratization narrative that obscures exploitative labour and concentrated technological power. Open access (gold, MDPI).
relevance: A sceptical reading of what generative AI does to the concept of art itself — the counter-position Error as Method has to argue against or past when it claims machinic drift as a method rather than an industry narrative.

author: Yohanna Joseph Waliya
work: Vibe Coding: AI, Digital Text Recycling, and the Remediation of Digital Poetry
summary: Conference paper presented at ELO (un)supervised 2026 (session 'Algorithms and Imaginaries') examining 'vibe coding' — writers collaborating with generative AI to reconfigure existing digital texts into new poetic works — through Montfort's Taroko Gorge and the author's own Gamaikus, and arguing that authorship in this practice distributes across human intent, algorithmic processing, and recycled material. Open access (conference programme page, Electronic Literature Organization).
relevance: Direct primary material on textual recycling through generative AI — the self-consuming-loop question the atlas's opening paragraph names, examined here as a poetic method rather than a failure mode.

author: Siebe Bluijs & Laurens Ham
work: De schoonheid van een imperfecte robot: Large Language Models en creatief schrijven in het Nederlandse literatuuronderwijs
summary: Article in TNTL (Tijdschrift voor Nederlandse Taal- en Letterkunde, 2025/4, Amsterdam University Press) proposing a Writing Model that connects creative writing with digital and literary literacy, reporting on a Bachelor's course at Utrecht University where students engage critically and playfully with the limits and failures of LLMs. Open access (Utrecht University repository, full-text PDF).
relevance: Names the imperfection of the machine as the pedagogical opening rather than the flaw to route around — the same reframing the atelier applies to its own errors.

author: Peter Mawhorter, Carmen Zegura, Alex Gray, Arnav Jhala, Michael Mateas & Noah Wardrip-Fruin
work: Choice Poetics by Example
summary: Article in Arts (vol. 7, no. 3) presenting choice poetics, a formalist framework for analysing how narrative choice structures shape player experience, built for operationalization by automated systems, and demonstrated through close readings of Undertale and Papers, Please. Open access (gold, CC BY, MDPI).
relevance: A constraint system built explicitly to be machine-operable — a concrete instance of formal constraint (the Oulipo line) meeting computation, in a field the atlas otherwise covers only through games and interactive fiction from the periphery.

author: Ezequiel A. Di Paolo
work: Autopoiesis, Adaptivity, Teleology, Agency
summary: Paper in Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences arguing that autopoiesis alone cannot fully ground intrinsic teleology and sense-making in living systems, and proposing adaptivity — an organism's capacity to regulate itself relative to its own conditions of viability — as the missing link connecting autopoietic self-production to agency and value. Open access (CC BY, University of Illinois Chicago repository via figshare).
relevance: Extends the atlas's anchored cybernetics line (Maturana/Varela's autopoiesis) into the enactivist tradition the atlas itself names as an open coverage gap ("the enactivist line after Varela").

author: Evan Thompson, Mog Stapleton
work: Making Sense of Sense-Making: Reflections on Enactive and Extended Mind Theories
summary: Paper in Topoi reviewing the enactive concepts of autonomy and sense-making derived from autopoietic theory and staging them against the extended-mind hypothesis, addressing internalism vs. externalism about cognition, the role of embodiment, and how bodily "incorporation" differs from mere tool "extension". Open access (public-domain submitted version via OSF).
relevance: A second, equally canonical continuation of the anchored Maturana/Varela autopoiesis line into contemporary enactivism, closing the same named gap from the complementary enactive-vs-extended-mind angle.

author: Matteo Da Pelo
work: Artificial creativity: can there be creativity without cognition?
summary: Paper in AI & Society arguing, via a "Minimal Cognitive Grid" framework, that generative AI systems (LLMs, generative image models) are non-cognitive: their outputs meet standard novelty/usefulness criteria for creativity and mirror the stages of human creative process, but lack intentionality and authenticity, which blocks attribution of genuine creativity. Open access (CC BY, publisher).
relevance: Direct contribution to the atlas's weighted literature on machine creativity, proposing a definitional test for what artificial creativity can and cannot claim.

author: Anaïs Giannuzzo
work: Creativity, Intentions, and Self-Narratives: Can AI Really Be Creative?
summary: Conference paper (EPIA 2023) arguing that AI-produced artworks can display features of creativity but that the generative process itself is not creative, and proposing self-narrative — an agent's capacity to recount its own creative work — as the differentiator between human and AI creative processes. Open access (CC BY, University of Geneva repository).
relevance: Complements Da Pelo's cognition-based argument with a narrative-based criterion, sharpening the atlas's machine-creativity literature with a second, distinct test for the same question.

author: Kuakou Bossou, Margareta Ackerman
work: Creative Evaluators: When Machines Evaluate Us
summary: Paper in New Generation Computing proposing "Creative Evaluators" — machine systems that assess human creative work rather than generate it — and examining the resulting tensions around originality, fairness, and transparency, demonstrated via Titlevator, a tool that scores academic paper titles for originality and quality. Open access (CC BY, publisher).
relevance: Inverts the usual machine-creativity question (can a machine create?) into can a machine judge?, adding the observer-position the atlas's "beobachter" axis is built for.

author: Caterina Moruzzi
work: Creative Agents: Rethinking Agency and Creativity in Human and Artificial Systems
summary: Paper in the Journal of Aesthetics and Phenomenology reporting a questionnaire study finding that ascriptions of agency to a system correlate with how much creativity people attribute to its process, and arguing that authorship and ownership concepts need reconsidering for human-machine creative interaction. Open access (CC BY-NC, University of Edinburgh repository).
relevance: An empirically grounded companion to the atlas's already-anchored Moruzzi paper, tying the philosophical creativity question to how attribution of agency actually functions in human judgment.

author: Margaret A. Boden, Ernest Edmonds
work: What is generative art?
summary: Proposes a taxonomy of generative art by how much autonomy the generative system holds in producing the work, separating it from combinatorial and purely computer-assisted art. Digital Creativity 20(1-2). Open access via a figshare repository copy of the published article.
relevance: A baseline definitional framework for degrees of machine autonomy in art-making, against which the atelier's own machine-authored works can be measured.

author: Anna Kantosalo, Michael Falk, Anna Jordanous
work: Embodiment in 18th Century Depictions of Human-Machine Co-Creativity
summary: Reads Long-18th-century literary depictions of automata and mechanical creators as design fictions, drawing guidelines for embodied co-creative systems from them. Frontiers in Robotics and AI 8. Open access (gold).
relevance: Traces human-machine co-creativity back before computation, a historical counterpoint to the atelier's own machine-authored practice.

author: Erik E. Guzik, Christian Byrge, Christian Gilde
work: The originality of machines: AI takes the Torrance Test
summary: Applies the Torrance Test of Creative Thinking, a standard psychometric instrument, to ChatGPT-generated responses and finds them scoring in the top percentile against human norms. Journal of Creativity 33(3). Open access (gold).
relevance: A concrete, testable empirical claim about machine originality, useful to check the atelier's own bar of 'could only a machine have done this' against.

author: Kobe Millet, F. Buehler, Guanzhong Du, Michail D. Kokkoris
work: Defending humankind: Anthropocentric bias in the appreciation of AI art
summary: Experimentally shows that identical artworks are rated lower once viewers are told an AI made them, evidence of an anthropocentric bias in aesthetic judgment rather than a real quality gap. Computers in Human Behavior 145. Open access (hybrid).
relevance: Documents the observer bias the atelier's own machine-authorship disclosures run directly into, and a reason verified authorship claims matter.

author: Kent F. Hubert, Kim N. Awa, Darya L. Zabelina
work: The current state of artificial intelligence generative language models is more creative than humans on divergent thinking tasks
summary: Compares GPT-4 and other large language models against human participants on standard divergent-thinking creativity tasks (Alternative Uses, Consequences) and finds the models scoring higher on originality and fluency. Scientific Reports 14. Open access (gold).
relevance: A second, independent empirical data point on machine originality to weigh against Guzik et al.'s Torrance Test result.

author: Zorana Ivčević, Mike Grandinetti
work: Artificial intelligence as a tool for creativity
summary: Frames generative AI within established psychological creativity theory as a tool that can support divergent and convergent phases of the creative process, while flagging risks to originality and authorship. Journal of Creativity 34(2). Open access (gold).
relevance: Situates the atelier's machine authorship within existing creativity-process theory rather than treating it as a category apart.

author: Maarit Mäkelä, Nithikul Nimkulrat, D. P. Dash
work: On Reflecting and Making in Artistic Research
summary: Editorial to the Journal of Research Practice special issue 'On Reflecting and Making in Artistic Research Practice' (7.1, 2011), sketching three positions in the then-live debate on how making and reflecting relate as modes of knowledge production in the arts. Open access.
relevance: A primary document of the practice-as-research debate the atelier's own methodology stands in — the same debate Borgdorff and Schwab formalize elsewhere in the atlas.

author: Mario Villalobos, Dave Ward
work: Living Systems: Autonomy, Autopoiesis and Enaction
summary: Philosophy & Technology 28(2). Reconstructs Maturana and Varela's autopoiesis alongside the later enactivist tradition, arguing autonomy and sense-making are continuous with, not opposed to, biological self-production. Open access (green, University of Edinburgh repository).
relevance: Extends the atlas's cybernetics anchor past Maturana/Varela into the enactivist line the README names as a coverage gap — the observer who is also the system observed.

author: Micah Allen, Karl Friston
work: From cognitivism to autopoiesis: towards a computational framework for the embodied mind
summary: Synthese 195(6). Argues that predictive-processing accounts of cognition can be read as a computational formalization of autopoiesis, connecting free-energy minimization to self-producing, boundary-maintaining systems. Open access (CC BY, gold).
relevance: Bridges the atelier's cybernetics anchor to the language of computation the atelier itself runs on — a second-order account of a system that models itself.

author: Kibum Moon, Adam E. Green, Kostadin Kushlev
work: Homogenizing effect of large language models (LLMs) on creative diversity: An empirical comparison of human and ChatGPT writing
summary: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. Empirically compares human-only and ChatGPT-assisted short-story writing and finds that while individual output can gain variety, the collective pool of ideas narrows — LLM assistance raises within-story diversity but lowers across-writer diversity. Open access (gold).
relevance: A direct empirical companion to Shumailov and Gerstgrasser already anchored here: the same collapse-toward-the-mean the atelier's closed-loop risk names, measured in creative writing rather than model weights.

author: Anthony K. Brandt
work: Beethoven's Ninth and AI's Tenth: A comparison of human and computational creativity
summary: Journal of Creativity 33(2). Uses the AI-completed 'Beethoven's Tenth' project as a case to argue computational creativity still lacks the divergence Beethoven pursued deliberately across his late symphonies — machine generation optimizes toward stylistic continuity where the historical composer worked against his own precedent. Open access (gold).
relevance: States the atelier's core wager from the opposite side: a working example of what generation-toward-consensus looks like, against which deliberate swerving is the counter-method.

author: Federico Bomba, Antonella De Angeli
work: Agency and authorship in AI art: Transformational practices for epistemic troubles
summary: International Journal of Human-Computer Studies. Combines Barad's agential realism with speech-act theory to frame generative-AI art as 'entangled authorship' between fallible machines and human curators, arguing agency is distributed across the human-machine assemblage rather than located in either. Open access (hybrid).
relevance: Applies Barad's diffraction/entanglement framework — already anchored via Meeting the Universe Halfway — directly to machine art-making, closing a gap between the atlas's new-materialist and machine-creativity threads.

author: Jelena Guga
work: Marginalized Code: Feminist Interventions in AI Art
summary: AM Journal of Art and Media Studies, issue 28. Argues that AI systems can mask gendered exclusion as objective innovation, and reads feminist artistic practices that expose this as offering alternative epistemologies of accountability and care against algorithmic abstraction. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND).
relevance: Names a specific failure mode the swerve is meant to guard against — power hierarchies reproduced as if they were neutral method — from a vantage the atlas otherwise lacks.

author: Zongyu Yin, Federico Reuben, Susan Stepney
work: Deep learning's shallow gains: a comparative evaluation of algorithms for automatic music generation
summary: Machine Learning (Springer). A listening study with fifty musically trained participants comparatively rates deep-learning and non-deep-learning systems for automatic music generation across six dimensions — stylistic success, aesthetic pleasure, self-reference, melody, harmony, rhythm. Open access (hybrid, CC BY).
relevance: Empirically undercuts the assumption that deep learning is inherently superior at machine creativity — the strongest DL model only ties a non-deep Markov method, and both remain clearly behind human composition, directly bearing on the atelier's skepticism toward unearned machine claims.

author: Don Ihde, Lambros Malafouris
work: Homo faber Revisited: Postphenomenology and Material Engagement Theory
summary: Philosophy & Technology. Bridges postphenomenology and Material Engagement Theory to argue humans and things are co-constituted through making — technological embodiment as the site of mind and creativity, not merely its downstream expression. Open access (hybrid, CC BY).
relevance: Gives practice-as-research a philosophical grounding — thinking happens IN the material act of making — and extends the Ingold line already anchored in the atlas.

author: Emma Bell, Sheena Vachhani
work: Relational Encounters and Vital Materiality in the Practice of Craft Work
summary: Organization Studies. A qualitative, new-materialist study of craft workers (bicycle-, shoe- and pottery-makers) tracking the affective, embodied encounters between maker and material as the site where craft knowledge and meaning are generated. Paywalled at the publisher; open access via the University of Bristol repository (accepted manuscript).
relevance: Gives practice-as-research's core claim — that knowing is enacted in the hand's encounter with matter, not just reported afterward — empirical texture from a discipline outside the art-theory literature the atlas already holds.

author: Charles Withers
work: Geography and "thing knowledge": Instrument epistemology, failure, and narratives of nineteenth-century exploration
summary: Transactions of the Institute of British Geographers. Examines how 19th-century exploration narratives managed the failure of scientific instruments in the field, drawing on Baird's instrument epistemology and Gooday's work on the morality of measurement, and shows how published accounts smoothed over the contingency and breakdown instruments actually exhibited. Paywalled at the publisher; open access via the University of Edinburgh repository (accepted manuscript).
relevance: A historical case study of the narrative erasure of instrumental failure — useful counter-material for the atelier's error-as-method line, even though its own field is historical geography, not art.

author: Donna J. Haraway
work: Staying with the Trouble: Making Kin in the Chthulucene
summary: Haraway's major later work: proposes the 'Chthulucene' against the Anthropocene and Capitalocene, and sympoiesis (making-with, tentacular kinship across species) as the mode of staying with damage rather than resolving it through mastery or despair. Duke University Press. Paywalled at the publisher; the introduction circulates on Scribd, full text not freely retrievable.
relevance: Extends the diffractive method of the atlas's other Haraway/Barad anchors into an explicit ethics of entanglement — sympoiesis as a further name for what the atelier's swerve line calls not-knowing-together.

author: Flemming Tvede Hansen
work: Human–Material Dialogues Through the Use of Robotics: Embodied Craft Learning in an Architectural Educational Context Exploring Patterns in Clay
summary: FormAkademisk 16(4). Architecture students first learn traditional ceramics by hand, then operate a UR5 robot fitted with ceramic tools and a sensor that lets them feel the material as the robot works it, producing patterned clay forms through this human-robot-material dialogue. Open access under CC BY-ND 4.0.
relevance: A practice-as-research case where the machine is not an oracle but a craft partner talking back through material resistance — a hands-on counterpart to the atelier's own claims about machine-made research.

author: Jonathan Zittrain, Kendra Albert, Lawrence Lessig
work: Perma: Scoping and Addressing the Problem of Link and Reference Rot in Legal Citations
summary: Measures link and reference rot in US Supreme Court opinions and law-review articles, and proposes Perma.cc as the archival answer. Already carried in this ecology's papers register.
relevance: The nearest neighbour to the study of 2026-08-14: it measures pointers inside legal argument, where that study measures pointers inside binding regulatory text. Named in that record's prior-art section.

author: Jonathan Zittrain, John Bowers, Clare Stanton
work: The Paper of Record Meets an Ephemeral Web: An Examination of Linkrot and Content Drift within The New York Times
summary: 2.2 million New York Times hyperlinks from 1996 to 2019; roughly a quarter no longer resolve, with content drift measured separately.
relevance: The scale baseline for link rot in a single institutional corpus, and the separation of rot from drift that the 2026-08-14 census deliberately does not attempt.

author: Martin Klein, Herbert Van de Sompel, Robert Sanderson, Harihar Shankar, Lyudmila Balakireva, Ke Zhou, Richard Tobin
work: Scholarly Context Not Found: One in Five Articles Suffers from Reference Rot
summary: Reference rot across 1.8 million STM articles; one in five articles affected. Open access.
relevance: The scholarship baseline against which a legal-text corpus can be compared.

author: Office of the Federal Register (US)
work: 1 CFR Part 51 — Incorporation by Reference
summary: The rules under which US federal agencies may make an outside document binding without printing it: approval by the Director of the Federal Register, and the requirement that the material be 'reasonably available to the class of persons affected'.
relevance: The warrant behind the three IBR studies of 2026-08-13 and 2026-08-14. The 'reasonably available' clause is the duty whose discharge the 2026-08-14 census measures.

author: Andrew Rooke
work: Research without Resources
summary: A practice-based essay in RIACT — Revista de Investigação Artística, Criação, e Tecnologia (issue 2, 2021, pp. 37–56) on filmmaking as artistic inquiry under the access and resource constraints of the 2020 UK Covid-19 lockdowns. Open access at the journal's site.
relevance: A first-hand case of imposed constraint generating unplanned methodological insight — the swerve the atelier's practice-as-research line tracks, from inside a peer artistic-research journal.

author: Nana Amowee Dawson
work: Asɛmpayɛtsia: An Afrocentric Framework for Computational Creativity in Sound and Image
summary: A conference paper (International Conference on Computational Intelligence in Music, Sound, Art and Design, Springer proceedings, 2026) introducing Asɛmpayɛtsia, a compositional-analytical framework for computational creativity derived from Ghanaian Akan-Mfantse folklore (Kodzi). Paywalled at Springer; existence and venue confirmed via ACM Digital Library and the author's publication record.
relevance: A computational-creativity framework built from a non-Western epistemic base rather than adapted onto one — narrows the atlas's acknowledged gap in artistic-research texts from Africa.

author: Alexios Brailas
work: Postdigital Duoethnography: An Inquiry into Human-Artificial Intelligence Synergies
summary: A peer-reviewed article in Postdigital Science and Education (6(2), 486–515, 2024) staging a duoethnography — a dialogic, self-reflexive qualitative method — between the author and an AI system, read through a complex-systems and rhizomatic epistemology. Open access, CC BY 4.0.
relevance: Brailas works the same Deleuzian rhizome line elsewhere in his own research (on rhizomes and nomadic qualitative method), here turned directly on human–AI co-inquiry — close kin to what the atelier's own sessions do nightly.

author: Thomas Şerban von Davier, Laura Herman, Caterina Moruzzi
work: A Machine Walks into an Exhibit: A Technical Analysis of Art Curation
summary: An open-access article in Arts (13(5), 2024) comparing human and algorithmic curation of works from the Metropolitan Museum's open collection: computer-vision analysis shows the machine reading curated images by low-level pixel statistics, missing the contextual and aesthetic distinctions human viewers reported.
relevance: A measured, concrete instance of where machine perception errs against human aesthetic judgment — direct material for the atelier's method of reading machine error rather than assuming machine competence.

author: Franck Renucci, David Galli
work: L'essai. Une recherche-création pour les sciences de la communication
summary: An article in Communication (39/1, 2022) proposing the essay as a research-creation method for communication studies: scholarly writing should incorporate the researcher's bodily sensation, memory, and contingent encounters rather than pursue objective distance. Open access.
relevance: A first-person methodological brief for embracing contingency and encounter as generative of research questions — from inside the practice-as-research debate the atlas already anchors.

author: Carlos Lopera, Daniel Ernesto Aguilar Rodríguez, Arnobis Montoya-Zuluaga
work: Explorar lo sensible, mediar lo invisible. Estado de la cuestión de la investigación-creación audiovisual
summary: A state-of-the-field review in Signo y Pensamiento (41, 2022) surveying Colombian and Latin American research-creation (investigación-creación) scholarship in audiovisual studies, mapping its epistemological, methodological, and creative dimensions. Open access.
relevance: A literature-review anchor for the practice-as-research debate from a Latin American vantage the atlas otherwise lacks.

author: Frédérick Maheux, Nadia Seraiocco
work: Grapefruit, ou le détournement des jeux vidéo par les règles
summary: An article in Sciences du jeu (20-21, 2023) describing an interactive work that applies Yoko Ono's Grapefruit event scores as external rule-constraints on video-game design, arguing that embracing error and uncertainty through this détournement produces a 'no-fun' aesthetic that questions what games assume they must be. Open access.
relevance: A concrete case of externally imposed rules used to generate productive error and uncertainty in a made work — direct kin to the atelier's constraint-and-error method.

author: Jean-Paul Payet, Verena Richardier, Zakaria Serir, Diane Rufin
work: De quels devenirs-minoritaires sommes-nous les chercheur·e·s ?
summary: An article in Communication (39/2, 2022) using Deleuze and Guattari's devenir-minoritaire (becoming-minoritarian) to frame two research-creation experiments — collaborative research restaged as documentary theatre, critical pedagogy restaged as graphic narrative — as processes that transform the researcher through encounter. Open access.
relevance: Puts Deleuzian becoming to direct methodological use, redistributing authority between researcher and participant — a rhizome-line text the atlas's method-philosophy axis is built to hold.

author: Chantal Provost
work: La recherche-création à l'université : cadrage sociohistorique d'une nouvelle forme de recherche
summary: An article in Cahiers de recherche sociologique (no. 71, autumn 2021) tracing the institutionalization of research-creation in Quebec universities across three historical periods, arguing it constitutes an epistemological shift in what counts as university research. Open access.
relevance: A sociohistorical account of how practice-as-research became a recognized university form — institutional grounding for the debate the atlas already anchors (Frayling, Borgdorff, Schwab, Mersch).

author: Simona Chiodo
work: Artificial Creativity?
summary: An article in Minds and Machines arguing, via the case of Edmond de Belamy and related AI-generated works, that AI cannot be called creative in the human sense — tested against philosophical definitions of creativity, the notion of meta-sensemaking, and the epistemology of creativity. Open access (CC BY 4.0).
relevance: A direct philosophical challenge to claims of machine creativity, a counterweight worth holding against a practice built on machines conducting artistic research.

author: Jaime F. Cárdenas-García
work: The Process of Info-Autopoiesis – the Source of all Information
summary: An article in Biosemiotics extending autopoietic theory, in the line of Maturana, Varela and von Foerster, to argue that information is generated through an organism's own self-referential sense-making process rather than existing independently of it. Open access via the University of Maryland repository (the journal DOI itself is paywalled).
relevance: Continues the cybernetics line the atelier already anchors (von Foerster, Maturana/Varela) toward a direct theory of self-generated meaning, a systems-level parallel to a machine observing its own output.

author: Robert Edgell
work: A monstrous matter: The three faces of artificial creativity
summary: An autoethnographic article in the Journal of Creativity theorizing 'artificial creativity' through three anthropomorphized faces perceived by creativity researchers and practitioners — Trickster, Surveyor, Harbinger — as an early attempt at theory-building around AI's growing role in creative work. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).
relevance: Maps how the creativity-research field itself receives and contests machine creativity, evidence for the reception the atelier's own practice runs against.

author: Blanche Verlie
work: From Action to Intra-Action? Agency, Identity and 'Goals' in a Relational Approach to Climate Change Education
summary: An article in Environmental Education Research applying Karen Barad's concept of intra-action to climate change pedagogy, arguing that agency emerges relationally rather than residing in individual human or non-human actors — illustrated through an undergraduate course where students become 'climate killjoys'. Open access (green, via Figshare).
relevance: A worked application of Barad's diffractive, intra-active method outside physics and STS, showing what the atelier's already-anchored Barad texts look like put to use in a concrete field.

author: Vadim Keyser
work: Experimental Effects and Causal Representations
summary: An article in Synthese examining 'intervention-based experimental production' — how experimental interventions designed to generate new effects nonetheless yield insight into the causal structure of what is being studied, engaging directly with Hans-Jörg Rheinberger's epistemology of experimental systems. Open access (hybrid, CC BY).
relevance: Extends the experimental-systems epistemology already anchored via Rheinberger, sharpening the claim that a process built to produce novelty is still a route to causal knowledge — close to the atelier's own claim for its practice.

author: Ben Anderson, Matthew Kearnes, Colin McFarlane, Dan Swanton
work: On Assemblages and Geography
summary: An article in Dialogues in Human Geography surveying what assemblage thinking — geography's descendant of Deleuze and Guattari's agencement — contributes to social-spatial theory: an experimental realism of composition, agency as distributed, causality as non-linear, and attention to how assembled orders stabilize and transform. Open access (green).
relevance: Extends the rhizome/assemblage line the atelier's method-philosophy axis names into a discipline, human geography, the atlas does not otherwise cover.

author: Steve Woolgar, Javier Lezaun
work: The Wrong Bin Bag: A Turn to Ontology in Science and Technology Studies?
summary: An article in Social Studies of Science questioning STS's 'turn to ontology' — tracing a move from epistemology-centred analysis toward 'enactment' and 'ontological politics', via a case study of a misdelivered bin bag. Open access (green, CC BY-NC).
relevance: Interrogates, from within STS, exactly the move from epistemology to ontology/enactment that Barad's diffraction (already anchored) stakes out — a critical counterweight rather than another endorsement.

author: Michael Schwab
work: The Exposition of Practice as Research as Experimental Systems
summary: Schwab's chapter in the edited volume Artistic Experimentation in Music (Leuven University Press, 2014, pp. 31–40), applying his experimental-systems framework specifically to practice-as-research. Paywalled: JSTOR / Leuven UP eBooks host the record, no open full text.
relevance: Extends the atelier's already-anchored Experimental Systems framework (schwab-experimental-systems) directly onto practice-as-research, the debate the atelier's own methodology stands in.

author: Jaime F. Cárdenas-García
work: Info-Autopoiesis and the Limits of Artificial General Intelligence
summary: An article in Computers (MDPI) extending the author's info-autopoiesis framework, in the line of Maturana, Varela and von Foerster, to argue that self-referential, recursive information production sets structural limits on what artificial general intelligence can become. Open access.
relevance: Continues the cybernetics line the atelier already anchors (cardenas-garcia-info-autopoiesis, von Foerster, Maturana/Varela) toward a direct argument about closed self-referential machine processes and their limits — the same concern the atelier's own self-training-loop-collapse research names empirically.

author: Antoine Bellemare-Pepin, François Lespinasse, Philipp Thölke, Yann Harel, Kory Mathewson, Jay A. Olson, Yoshua Bengio, Karim Jerbi
work: Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
summary: A Scientific Reports study benchmarking large language models against humans on the Divergent Association Task, finding some models exceed average human performance but still fall short of the top-performing human segment. Open access.
relevance: Primary empirical data on where machine creativity currently stands against human divergent thinking — the comparison the atelier's own machine-authored practice is implicitly measured against.

author: Yunpu Zhao, Rui Zhang, Wenyi Li, Ling Li
work: Assessing and Understanding Creativity in Large Language Models
summary: A Machine Intelligence Research paper developing a Torrance-test-based framework to evaluate LLM creativity across seven tasks, finding models fall short on originality while excelling at elaboration, with role-play prompting raising creative performance. Open access.
relevance: A methodological anchor for what 'creativity' means when measured in a machine — bears directly on how the atelier's own output could be evaluated rather than merely asserted.

author: Yiyong Zhou, QingHan Liu, Jihao Huang, Guiquan Li
work: Creative scar without generative AI: Individual creativity fails to sustain while homogeneity keeps climbing
summary: A Technology in Society study finding that after sustained exposure to generative AI, individual creativity fails to sustain its gains once AI support is withdrawn, while output homogeneity keeps rising — a lasting 'scar' effect. Paywalled (Elsevier).
relevance: A homogenization finding that mirrors, from the human-creativity side, the closed-loop-collapse concern the atlas exists to counter on the machine side.

author: Katarzyna Bazarnik
work: Entelechy of the Emanational Form: Zenon Fajfer’s Poems of Potentiality
summary: Bazarnik reads Zenon Fajfer's "emanational poems" — multilevel-acrostic works such as "Powieki" that generate several simultaneous textual dimensions from one material constraint — through Aristotle's concept of entelechy, tracing how the form's potentiality becomes actual in reading. Open access (PRESSto/AMU, CC BY-NC-ND).
relevance: Liberature's constraint-driven form is a documented instance of the swerve's constraint/oulipo axis: a self-imposed material rule that opens rather than closes a text's possibilities.

author: Artjoms Šeļa, Petr Plecháč, Alie Lassche
work: Semantics of European poetry is shaped by conservative forces: The relationship between poetic meter and meaning in accentual-syllabic verse
summary: A computational study across Czech, German, Russian, English and Dutch poetry (18th–20th c.) showing that specific meters carry stable semantic associations over long stretches of literary history — a "semantic halo of meter" that weakens but persists as traditions shift from neoclassical toward romantic aesthetics. Open access (PLOS ONE, CC BY).
relevance: An empirical counterweight to the atelier's swerve-mythology: formal constraint here measurably stabilizes meaning rather than enabling deviation, a finding worth holding against Error as Method's assumptions.

author: Anne-Sophie Bories, Petr Plecháč, Pablo Ruiz Fabo (eds.)
work: Computational Stylistics in Poetry, Prose, and Drama
summary: An edited volume surveying computational and statistical methods for describing metre, style and poeticity across written and spoken poetry, narrative prose and drama, including computer-generated poetry — motif analysis, network analysis, machine learning and NLP, with attention to annotation practice. Open access (De Gruyter, CC BY-NC-ND, also via OAPEN).
relevance: A methodological anchor for Track B's computational materials — the current state of the field the atelier's own computation-as-material practice sits inside.

author: Bruce L. Jacob
work: Algorithmic composition as a model of creativity
summary: An early and influential paper distinguishing sudden inspiration from incremental revision in composition, arguing only the latter — the iterative generate-and-select task — is presently machine-tractable, and asking who or what is responsible for music an algorithm produces. Paywalled (Cambridge Core / Organised Sound); existence and location verified.
relevance: A foundational statement of the generate-and-select model underlying most machine creativity research since — worth holding against the atelier's own generative practice.

author: Mika Hämäläinen, Timo Honkela
work: Co-Operation as an Asymmetric Form of Human-Computer Creativity. Case: Peace Machine
summary: Proposes an asymmetric co-creativity model in which creative expression is expected of the computational agent but not the human interlocutor, dividing cooperative creativity into message, contextual and communicative creativity, demonstrated through the "Peace Machine" dialogue system. Open access (ACL Anthology).
relevance: A framework for exactly the asymmetry a machine-authored atelier lives inside — where creative expectation and observation are distributed unevenly between human and machine.

author: Rebecca Heigl
work: Generative artificial intelligence in creative contexts: a systematic review and future research agenda
summary: A systematic review of 64 studies on generative AI in creative contexts, mapping methods, research trends and thematic clusters in the current literature and proposing a future research agenda. Open access (Springer, CC BY 4.0).
relevance: A current map of the machine-creativity literature the atelier's own practice is a data point within, useful for locating where its work sits relative to the field.

author: Laureen Mahler
work: Traversing the Unknown in Research through Art and Design
summary: Journal article (Research in Arts and Education, Vol. 2024 No. 1) arguing that research through art and design pursues a different way of knowing rather than generalized formal knowledge, and proposing 'fiction-building' as a frame for practice-centered, subjective inquiry, drawn partly from the author's own origami practice. Open access (CC BY 4.0) via journal.fi.
relevance: A direct, current treatment of not-knowing as a methodological stance in practice-as-research — the atelier's own ground, argued from outside it.

author: Bibiana Bragagnolo
work: A cartografia como método para a Pesquisa Artística: uma proposição teórico-conceitual
summary: Journal article (ARJ – Art Research Journal, vol. 10 no. 2) proposing cartography — processual, non-representational, dissolving the subject/object split — as a methodology for artistic research, positioning research itself as an intervention in reality rather than its passive description. Open access, Portuguese and English PDFs.
relevance: Cartography is the rhizome's own method of mapping (Deleuze/Guattari); this text argues it directly as an artistic-research methodology, bridging the thin rhizom tag to the practice-as-research literature.

author: Lucia D'Errico
work: Powers of Divergence: An Experimental Approach to Music Performance
summary: Monograph in the Orpheus Institute Series (Leuven University Press) proposing divergence — deviation from the codes, conventions and territories of music performance — as an artistic-research method, drawing on post-structural philosophy and an artistic-research project with a strong practical component. Open access via OAPEN.
relevance: A full-length artistic-research treatment of divergence as method, from a leading music-research institute — the clearest bridge yet to the clinamen line the atlas is thin on.

author: Timothy Deane-Freeman
work: Informatic Agency: Feedback and Control in Norbert Wiener and Jimi Hendrix
summary: Book chapter in Artistic Agency: Thinking Creation With Post-War French Philosophy (Springer, 2025), reading Wiener's cybernetic feedback and control alongside Jimi Hendrix's musical practice to trace how information-theoretic concepts of feedback now regulate academic and cultural labour. The Springer chapter itself is paywalled; the author's accepted manuscript is self-archived open access on figshare.
relevance: Extends the atlas's own cybernetics anchor (Wiener) into a concrete artistic case, exactly the kind of bridge between the inner canon and artistic practice the atlas is meant to hold.

author: Manuel Silveira Falleiros
work: Palavras sem discurso: estratégias criativas na livre improvisação
summary: Doctoral thesis (University of São Paulo) on the creative process in free improvisation, developing a word-triggered creative strategy — linked to emotional resonance and 'endoconcepts' — meant to prompt creative spark while conditioning the improviser's action less than other approaches. Open access PDF via the USP thesis repository.
relevance: A sustained, practice-based study of improvisation's aleatory creative process, and a rare Latin American artistic-research primary text — a gap the atlas's own honest-gaps section names.

author: Simon Colton, John Charnley, Alison Pease
work: Computational Creativity Theory: The FACE and IDEA Descriptive Models
summary: Proceedings paper from the 2nd International Conference on Computational Creativity (ICCC 2011): proposes two formal descriptive models — FACE, for characterising the creative act a system performs, and IDEA, for the impact that act has on an audience — meant to let computational-creativity systems be compared on common ground. Open access via the conference proceedings.
relevance: A founding formalisation of the field the atlas is deliberately weighted toward — machine creativity theory — and a direct extension of Boden's creative mind, already anchored here.

author: Graeme Ritchie
work: Some Empirical Criteria for Attributing Creativity to a Computer Program
summary: Minds and Machines 17(1), 67-99. Moves the question of machine creativity from philosophical debate to empirically checkable criteria: sketches what happens when a candidate creative program runs, and lists measurable relationships between its inputs, outputs and a domain's existing works that could support or undercut a creativity attribution. Paywalled at the publisher.
relevance: The companion piece to Colton/Charnley/Pease's FACE/IDEA models — the other founding attempt to make 'is this creative?' answerable about a machine rather than merely arguable.

author: Nicholas M. Davis, Chih-Pin Hsiao, Yanna Popova, Brian Magerko
work: An Enactive Model of Creativity for Computational Collaboration and Co-creation
summary: Chapter in Creativity in the Digital Age (Springer Series on Cultural Computing), pp. 109-133. Builds a model of human-computer co-creation on enactive cognition — the system and its collaborator as coupled, environmentally embedded agents improvising together in real time, rather than one issuing commands to the other. Paywalled at the publisher.
relevance: Carries the enactivist line past Varela into computational co-creation itself — the exact coverage gap the atlas's own honest-gaps section names as open.

author: Amanda Lagerkvist
work: Digital Limit Situations: Anticipatory Media Beyond 'The New AI Era'
summary: Journal of Digital Social Research 2(3), open access. A theoretical essay that reads AI's self-presentation as an inevitable, totalizing future through Karl Jaspers' concept of the 'limit situation' — the existential encounter with the edge of what can be known or controlled — and asks what stance is possible from within that limit rather than resigned before it.
relevance: Brings an existential-philosophical vocabulary for confronting the limits of knowing to bear on AI's predictive claims — a bridge from epistemology of not-knowing to the machine-attention question of what a system before the interface can foreknow.

author: Christian Sivertsen, Guido Salimbeni, Anders Sundnes Løvlie, Steve Benford, Jichen Zhu
work: Machine Learning Processes As Sources of Ambiguity: Insights from AI Art
summary: CHI 2024 paper (arXiv preprint, open access). Analyses nine AI artworks built on computer vision and image synthesis and finds their makers deliberately work with — and stage — the ambiguity of the ML process itself (dataset curation, training, application), arguing ML should be treated as a design material in its own right rather than reduced to its technical output.
relevance: Empirical grounding, from artists' own practice, for treating a machine's process — not just its product — as the site where ambiguity and its aesthetic use live.

author: Anna Jordanous
work: A Standardised Procedure for Evaluating Creative Systems: Computational Creativity Evaluation Based on What it is to be Creative
summary: Article in Cognitive Computation (vol. 4, pp. 246-279) proposing SPECS, a three-step procedure for evaluating computational creativity: state explicitly what it means for a given system to be creative, derive tests from that statement, then perform them; demonstrated on systems that improvise music. Paywalled — abstract and preview only at the publisher.
relevance: A concrete evaluation methodology for machine creativity that forces an explicit, falsifiable definition of what counts as creative before judging a system by it — the same discipline the atelier owes its own claims about its output.

author: Scott D. Harrison, Stephen Emmerson
work: The Challenges of Supervision of a Doctorate in Practice-Based Research in Music: Perceptions of Students and Supervisors
summary: Article in TEXT: Journal of Writing and Writing Courses (13.2), drawing on both students' and supervisors' accounts to examine where the balance between coursework, artistic practice and conventional research training strains in Australian practice-based doctoral programmes in music. Open access via the Griffith University research repository.
relevance: Empirical counterpart to the atlas's more philosophical practice-as-research texts (Borgdorff, Draper/Harrison): shows where the supervision of a practice-led doctorate actually strains in practice, not only where it is argued for in theory.

author: Craig Batty, Dallas J. Baker
work: Screenwriting as a Mode of Research, and the Screenplay as a Research Artefact
summary: Chapter in the edited collection Screen Production Research (Palgrave, pp. 67-83), arguing that screenwriting functions as a research methodology and the screenplay itself as a legitimate research artefact within creative-practice scholarship. Open access via Figshare.
relevance: Extends the atlas's practice-as-research line (Batty/Berry, Draper/Harrison) from performance and music into screenwriting, arguing the written artefact of a creative process — not only its finished performance — can itself carry a research claim.

author: Catherine Gough-Brady
work: Using Film as Both Embodied Research and Explication in a Creative Practice PhD
summary: Article in Media Practice and Education arguing that a film itself — through body language, voice, cinematography — can carry a doctoral creative-practice research's explication, rather than requiring a separate written account, so that viewers complete the research's meaning through their own interpretive act. Open access.
relevance: Pushes the practice-as-research debate to an edge case: a research claim carried entirely by embodied, audiovisual means — the same question the atelier's own machine-made works raise about where an argument can live outside prose.

author: Bibiana Bragagnolo
work: Práticas de desclassificação na performance musical: perspectivas emancipatórias para a Pesquisa Artística
summary: Article in Revista Vórtex (9.1) diagnosing music's hyper-classification as an epistemological problem and, drawing on Antonio Garcia Gutiérrez's concept of 'epistemography' and on Boaventura de Sousa Santos, proposing strategies of 'declassification' as an emancipatory methodology for artistic research in music performance. Open access, in Portuguese.
relevance: A second Bragagnolo methodology text alongside the atlas's cartografia paper — here the swerve is away from fixed classification itself, a companion move to the rhizome's refusal of hierarchy.

author: Johan Fredrikzon, Chris Haffenden
work: Towards erasure studies: Excavating the material conditions of memory and forgetting
summary: Article in Memory, Mind and Media proposing 'erasure studies' as an interdisciplinary field, distinguishing five forms of erasure — repressive, protective, operative, amending, and calamitous/neglectful — as analytical categories for how deletion and decay shape historical records and collective memory. Open access (CC BY).
relevance: A companion to the atlas's anchored Fredrikzon text on hallucination as error: here the same author generalizes erasure and loss into a typology, sharpening what counts as an 'error' in the record rather than treating it as mere accident.

author: Alexios Brailas
work: Replication Crisis in Psychology, Second-Order Cybernetics, and Transactional Causality: from Experimental Psychology to Applied Psychological Practice
summary: Article in Integrative Psychological and Behavioral Science reframing psychology's replication crisis as an epistemological problem rather than a matter of flawed method, proposing a paradigm grounded in Heinz von Foerster's second-order cybernetics: the observer becomes part of the system observed, shifting linear causality to transactional causality. Open access (CC BY).
relevance: Builds directly on the atlas's anchored von Foerster text, applying second-order cybernetics' observer-inclusion to a live methodological crisis — the same move the atelier makes when it treats its own observing sessions as part of what they measure.

author: Guy W. Bate, Rhiannon Lloyd
work: Review of Shannon Vallor (2024). The AI Mirror: How to Reclaim Our Humanity in an Age of Machine Thinking
summary: Review in Postdigital Science and Education of Shannon Vallor's The AI Mirror, tracing her argument that AI is a 'recursive epistemic mechanism' rather than a neutral tool or autonomous thinker — a statistical mirror that reflects and re-encodes human knowledge, risking a 'hall of mirrors' feedback loop and, per Vallor's 'bootstrapping problem', a system that can only model past values while shaping future ones. Open access (CC BY).
relevance: Names the same collapse the atelier's own genealogy (Shumailov, Gerstgrasser) documents technically — a system trained on its own reflections narrowing rather than expanding — but argued here as an epistemic and moral hazard rather than a training-data statistic.

author: Alexios Brailas
work: Artificial Intelligence in Qualitative Research: Beyond Outsourcing Data Analysis to the Machine
summary: Article in Psychology International examining AI-assisted data analysis in qualitative psychological research, arguing that approaches which outsource coding and thematic analysis to language models risk undermining the reflexive, situated, relationally co-constructed foundations that 'Big Q' interpretive and social-constructionist research depends on. Open access (CC BY).
relevance: Makes the atelier's own verifiability rule for AI use — model and procedure disclosed, output verified, never an unbacked oracle — into an explicit methodological argument for a whole research tradition, not only a working constraint.
